narrative: A 24-year-old from Darayya, a suburb of Damascus at the center of intense fighting between the regime and rebels, finally reached Germany when the smuggler shouted, 'Out of the truck, we are in Munich.' He had met the other 20 Syrians only at the smuggler's house back in Budapest, and he did not know any of them. He had no good clothes, just dirty jeans and an ugly jacket, and expected the police to come at any moment. The driver told them to wait 15 minutes and then left. He decided to find the first police officer he could, but first met two Syrian men and a little boy from Damascus who suggested they go to Saarbruecken, where the procedures for refugees were said to be faster. They took a cab to the bus station, then a six-hour bus ride, most of which he slept through, hungry and exhausted. At the Saarbruecken refugee camp there were many nationalities, long lines and noise; he ate quickly and slept. The first full day was hard, waiting in lines for food and papers. After about a week he was transferred to a camp in Trier, smaller and so full that he spent the first night in a hallway, then was transferred again. By his 28th day in Germany he was used to the camps, sleeping in a tent with 200 people, the hardest part being the constant noise. Finally he was transferred to a house in the small town of Stadecken-Elsheim, where six people would live until their three-year residence visas came through. At the municipal office the staff smiled and were kind. A volunteer began teaching him German; he called her his German mother. He noticed that everyone smiled at them, but the refugees had seemed to forget how to smile. After ten months of waiting he received his residence visa, allowed to stay three years to work and study.
